bib.title: Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models", Maxwell Nye, Anders Johan Andreassen, Guy Gur-Ari, Henryk Michalewski, Jacob Austin, David Bieber, David Dohan, Aitor Lewkowycz, Maarten Bosma, David Luan, Charles Sutton, Augustus Odena (MIT; Google Research Brain and Blueshift). Preprint, arXiv:2112.00114v1, 30 Nov 2021.

COVERAGE: 50,465 of 50,465 chars. I read everything: body, limitations, Appendices A to D, and the Figure 7 caption on p16. I only skimmed the references. The extraction is clean.

**Main point for the target note.** The paper never says "40M" or any other threshold size in its text. Section 3 only says "beyond a critical model size". The size can only be read off the Figure 3 plot, whose x-axis runs over 10^7 to 10^9 parameters. So the note's "from about 40M" comes from the survey's reading of the plot, not from a number Nye et al. state. If the note cites Nye directly, phrase it as "beyond a critical size (around 10^7–10^8 in Fig. 3)", or keep the 40M attributed to the survey. Also, the scratchpad in the addition experiments is fine-tuned, not prompted. Few-shot scratchpad results exist only for polynomial evaluation and synthetic Python, both on the 137B model.

CLAIMS
- claim: On fine-tuned long addition, models above a critical size solve the task with a scratchpad. Models without one fail even at the largest size tested, and fail completely on 9–10 digit addition (out of distribution).
  number: none (the threshold is only shown in Fig. 3)
  setup: pre-trained decoder-only LMs from 2M to 1B params, fine-tuned on 100k examples of 1–8 digit addition for 5k steps at batch size 32. Test sets: 10k in-distribution examples and 1k for each OOD length.
  quote: "beyond a critical model size, models are able to solve the addition task using the scratchpad, while models trained without a scratchpad fail to do so even at the largest tested scale. On the out-of-distribution tasks (9-10 digit addition), we find that models trained without scratchpad completely fail"
  where: p4, Sec 3 Results
- claim: Addition setup details.
  number: 100k examples, 5k steps, batch 32, 2M–1B params
  quote: "The models were fine-tuned on 100k examples for 5k steps with batch size 32. There are 10k in-distribution test examples, and 1k test examples for each out-of-distribution task. We examine the performance as a function of model size, ranging from 2M to 1B parameters."
  where: p4
- claim: On polynomial evaluation the scratchpad beats direct prediction both few-shot and fine-tuned.
  number: few-shot 8.8% to 20.1%; fine-tuned 31.8% to 50.7%
  setup: polynomials of degree 3 or less, inputs in [-10,10], outputs in [-1000,1000], 10k train / 2k test. Few-shot uses the 137B model with n=4 examples. Fine-tuned uses an 8B model for 2000 steps.
  quote: "Few-shot Fine-tuning / Direct prediction 8.8% 31.8% / Scratchpad 20.1% 50.7%" and "a 137B parameter pre-trained decoder-only model ... We use n = 4 example problems in the few-shot prompt. We also evaluate in the fine-tuning regime with an 8B parameter model fine-tuned for 2000 steps"
  where: p4–5, Table 1
- claim: On synthetic Python programs, scratchpad tracing beats direct execution prediction few-shot and fine-tuned. The few-shot number needed a changed scoring rule; under naive scoring it is about zero.
  number: few-shot 11% to 26.5%*; fine-tuned 20% to 41.5%
  setup: 137B model with 1024-token context, 512-token generation limit and greedy decoding (T=0). 400/100/200 programs, 3 inputs each from 0–9. Few-shot prompt has 3 examples.
  quote: "Direct prediction 11% 20% / Scratchpad 26.5%* 41.5%" and "(Under naive scoring, the few-shot tracing accuracy is roughly zero.)"
  where: p6, Table 2, Sec 5.1
- claim: On real MBPP programs, the best scratchpad model (MBPP-aug + CodeNet + single line) gets the right output on 26.6% of tasks against 10.3% for direct execution trained on MBPP. Greedy decoding gives an exact trace for about 42% of traces.
  number: 26.6% vs 10.3% per-task; 46.0% vs 22.0% per-example; 41.9% per-example trace exact match
  setup: 137B model, 212 of the 500 MBPP eval tasks (those whose traces fit the 512-token generation window)
  quote: "per-task execution acc: 10.3 5.1 5.1 17.3 26.6 25.2 23.4" and "greedily decoding from the best model produces the exact correct trace for almost 42% of all traces."
  where: p8–9, Table 3
- claim: With very little data (374 MBPP tasks), the scratchpad does worse than direct execution.
  number: 5% vs 10%
  quote: "Neither the scratchpad model or the direct execution model achieve good performance (5% and 10% output accuracy, respectively), and direct execution outperforms the scratchpad model."
  where: p7, Sec 5.2.1
- claim: Augmenting with model-sampled programs (80 per task at T=0.5, about 17k new programs, executed by an interpreter) more than triples the tasks the scratchpad solves, but hurts direct execution.
  number: 5.1 to 17.3 (scratchpad); 10.3 to 5.1 (direct)
  quote: "While the direct execution approach suffers a decrease in accuracy when trained on this additional data, the performance of the scratchpad model is greatly improved; the model trained on the augmented data solves more than three times the number of tasks"
  where: p7
- claim: Ablation: fine-tuning a scratchpad model afterwards to answer directly gives no significant gain. The benefit is not only from the extra training signal; it comes from using the scratchpad at inference.
  number: none
  quote: "We see no significant benefits from doing any intermediate training using a scratchpad. This indicates that the extra training-time information seen by the scratchpad model does not seem solely responsible for the scratchpad model's improved performance."
  where: p13, App B; Fig 7 p16
- claim: Tracing fine-tuning costs some synthesis ability.
  number: 54% vs 62%
  quote: "achieved an overall synthesis accuracy of 54%, compared to the 62% accuracy of the original few-shot model in Austin et al. (2021)"
  where: p13, App A
- claim: The authors' reasons it works: adaptive compute time, intermediate state stored in context rather than in activations, states quantized to tokens so errors compound less, and inspectable errors.
  number: none
  quote: "First, the model has adaptive computation time ... Second, the model can store the intermediate state of its computation in the scratch buffer and refer back to it by attending to its context."
  where: p3

LIMITS: The addition results are fine-tuned only, up to 1B. There is no few-shot addition result, so the paper does not show a prompted-CoT scaling threshold. All few-shot results come from one 137B model (the Austin et al. 2021 family, trained on web and dialog data). There are no confidence intervals or repeated seeds. The few-shot synthetic score depends on a changed scoring criterion (App D). The MBPP evaluation drops more than half the tasks, keeping 212 of 500 whose traces fit 512 tokens. The authors concede context and generation window size as a limit ("we limit our experiments to problems where the scratchpad text fits within the model generation window (512 tokens)"). They also concede that scratchpads need hand-designed supervision; learning them without supervision, e.g. via RL, is left as future work. Dated: this predates Wei et al. 2022 CoT prompting, and the RL-to-learn-scratchpad idea anticipates later reasoning-model training.

BUILDS ON: Austin et al. (2021), the MBPP and direct execution baseline; Zaremba & Sutskever (2014), learning to execute; Bieber et al. (2020), synthetic programs; Graves et al. (2014) NTM and Graves (2016) ACT; Banino et al. (2021) PonderNet; Dehghani et al. (2018) universal transformers; Kurach et al. (2016); Kaiser & Sutskever (2016); Saxton et al. (2019), polynomial evaluation; Puri et al. (2021), CodeNet; Brown et al. (2020), GPT-3 failing at addition beyond 3 digits.

CODE (Figure 2, p3, the addition scratchpad target):
```
Input:
2 9 + 5 7
Target:
<scratch>
2 9 + 5 7 , C: 0
2 + 5 , 6 C: 1 # added 9 + 7 = 6 carry 1
, 8 6 C: 0 # added 2 + 5 + 1 = 8 carry 0
0 8 6
</scratch>
8 6
```
The comments are not part of the target. Digits are space-separated so each digit is its own token (footnote 2, p4). Figure 4 (p5) has a short polynomial scratchpad: `Evaluate -7*x**2 + 7*x + 5 at x = 1` then `<scratch> -7*x**2: -7 / 7*x: 7 / 5: 5 </scratch> total: 5`.

FIGURES:
- Fig 3, p4: "Using a scratchpad significantly improves the performance of pre-trained Transformer-based models on addition, including their ability to generalize out of the training distribution to numbers with more digits. Models were trained on 1-8 digit addition." Best candidate. Three accuracy-vs-parameter-count panels (in-distribution, 9 digits, 10 digits) show the critical-size jump and the flat-zero baseline at a glance. It is also the only source of the threshold.
- Fig 1, p2: direct execution prediction vs scratchpad line-by-line trace. Shows the idea in one picture.
- Fig 2, p3: addition scratchpad example (above). Makes "intermediate tokens" concrete.
- Fig 7, p16: ablation, scratchpad pre-training then direct answering. Shows that inference-time tokens matter, not just the extra supervision.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. Text extraction is clean, apart from mangled quote glyphs in the Fig 6 single-line examples ("/quotesingle.Var"). Table 3's multi-row header extracts flattened. Its columns, left to right, are: Direct MBPP, Direct MBPP-aug, Scratchpad MBPP, Scratchpad MBPP-aug, Scratchpad MBPP-aug+CodeNet+single line, MBPP-aug+CodeNet, MBPP-aug+single line. I matched them to the prose values (26.6, 25.2, 23.4). Plot values in Figs 3 and 7 cannot be quoted as text.
